description: Test your knowledge of MI3.10-13 | Blood & Tissue Parasites and HIV/AIDS with focus on malaria parasitology, life cycle, and clinical features.

cards.text: Which Plasmodium species causes quartan fever (72-hour cycle), and which RBCs does it prefer?
cards.answer: P. malariae causes quartan fever with 72-hour periodicity. It infects senescent (older) RBCs, producing the mildest form of malaria.

tip.tip: Malariae = Mellow fever (quartan, 4-day cycle); prefers old RBCs

cards.text: What are hypnozoites, and which Plasmodium species form them?
cards.answer: Hypnozoites are dormant liver forms that persist after the initial hepatic schizogony. P. vivax and P. ovale form hypnozoites, which reactivate months to years later causing relapse.

tip.tip: Hypno = sleep; only vivax & ovale do this; requires primaquine to eliminate

cards.text: Describe the classic malaria paroxysm and its three stages.
cards.answer: Cold stage (30-60 min): rigors & vasoconstriction. Hot stage (2-6 hr): high fever ≥40°C with headache & vomiting. Sweating stage (2-4 hr): profuse diaphoresis with defervescence.

tip.tip: Cold → Hot → Sweat (CHS). Merozoite burst → TNF-α/IL-1 → fever cycle

cards.text: Name two cytoadherence mechanisms that make P. falciparum malignant and cause sequestration.
cards.answer: PfEMP1 (P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1) on RBCs binds ICAM-1 and CD36 on endothelial cells. Rosetting occurs when infected RBCs clump with uninfected RBCs, blocking microvascular blood flow.

tip.tip: PfEMP1 = sticky protein; rosettes = flower-like clusters of cells

cards.text: What is blackwater fever, and why does it occur in severe P. falciparum malaria?
cards.answer: Blackwater fever is massive intravascular haemolysis resulting in haemoglobinuria (dark/cola-colored urine), often progressing to acute kidney injury. Caused by severe parasitaemia and immune-mediated RBC destruction.

tip.tip: Black water = haemoglobin in urine; indicates severe falciparum with high mortality if untreated

cards.text: Distinguish between relapse and recrudescence in malaria.
cards.answer: Relapse: P. vivax/ovale reactivation from hypnozoites weeks-months later; requires primaquine. Recrudescence: P. falciparum/malariae low-level persisting parasitaemia resurges; due to incomplete treatment, NOT dormant forms.

tip.tip: Relapse = reactivation from liver; Recrudescence = incomplete cure; Vivax/Ovale = Relapse

cards.text: Why does P. falciparum infect a higher proportion of RBCs than P. vivax or P. ovale?
cards.answer: P. falciparum can infect RBCs of all ages (young, mature, old), allowing 10-30% parasitaemia. P. vivax and P. ovale infect only reticulocytes, limiting parasitaemia to <1%, which is why falciparum causes severe disease.

tip.tip: Falciparum is democratic (all RBCs); Vivax/Ovale are selective (reticulocytes only) = milder

cards.text: What does 'Schüffner's dots' on peripheral smear indicate, and which species produce them?
cards.answer: Schüffner's dots are fine pink stippling on RBCs seen with certain stains. Produced by P. vivax and P. ovale, they indicate cytoplasmic inclusions and help differentiate benign malaria from falciparum (which shows Maurer's clefts).

tip.tip: Schüffner = fine dots (vivax/ovale); Maurer = coarse clefts (falciparum)
